newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU verdict on Anglo's Lonrho stake still in doubt.
newsitem.headline: EU verdict on Anglo's Lonrho stake still in doubt.

text.p: The European Commission's decision on Anglo American's controversial stake in Lonrho Plc is still in doubt, not the least because the case presents several legal uncertainties, lawyers and EU sources said on Friday.

The Commission's well-known position, made public by European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert, is that the Anglo, the South African mining giant, cannot keep its 28-percent stake unless it gives up control of Lonrho's platinum division.

This means that the platinum interests would have to be sold off, something the British conglomerate seems to be resisting. Another possible remedy is that Anglo reduces its stake to a level acceptable for the Commission.
"Anglo said publicly that it's not platinum they are interested in," a lawyer well-versed in EU competition law, said.

"But if Lonrho's division doesn't go, the shareholding will have to be reduced to levels where they will no longer have control," the lawyer, who asked not to be named, said. He thought 20 percent could be an acceptable level.
Another view, expressed by sources close to the companies, is that neither of this needs to happen.

The sources challenge the Commission's assessment that Anglo's stake gives it control of Lonrho. "It's a very low level of shareholdings. Anglo maintains that they do not control Lonrho," one source said.
There are also strong doubts as to whether the EU's merger regulation, which is being used to assess the impact of Anglo's stake on competition, is applicable.

In a move which could ultimately tear to pieces some Commission high-profile merger decisions in the past -- most notably its ban in 1996 of the proposed merger of the platinum interests of Lonrho itself and Gencor -- one European court advocate-general said recently that the application of the regulation to situations of collective dominance was questionable.
Gencor is appealing the Commission's veto.

Anglo's stake in Lonrho effectively puts the platinum market under the control of the two companies, on the one side, and Gencor Ltd of South Africa. Together they control 63 percent of the world's output and 90 percent of the world's reserves.
The merger regulation bans creation or strengthening of a dominant position.

The advocate general, Giuseppe Tesauro, was giving his opinion on an appeal against a Commission decision in 1993 to attach tough conditions to a German potash merger involving BASF subsidiary Kali + Salz and MdK. The deal left the EU's market in the hands of the merged company and France's Societe Commerciale des Potasses et de l'Azote (SCPA).

Tesauro's doubts concern Commission officials greatly. They are now hoping the European Court of Justice will make it clear the merger rules apply to duopolies and oligopolies before the deadline to rule on Anglo/Lonrho.
"We will have to wait; (Anglo) has plenty of time, we may not have to block it," an EU competition official told Reuters.
The Commission has until May 5 to take a final decision, following the opening in December of an in-depth investigation into Anglo's stake in the British-based conglomerate.

A Commission spokesman said earlier on Thursday that the next move ought to come from Anglo following a statement of objections sent to the company weeks ago. Earlier this week, other interested parties, including Anglo, had a chance to make their views known at a Commission hearing.
"The ball is in their camp...we'll see if they can come up with remedies we can accept," he said.
